title: The basic laws of chemistry
summary: Mass is conserved and ratios are fixed. Learn the basic laws that describe chemistry with numbers.
cards.0.p: Lavoisier weighed reactions in closed containers. He found that the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. Atoms are not destroyed or created from nothing. They are only rearranged.
cards.0.key: In a closed container, the total mass shown on the balance does not change during the reaction.
cards.0.once.soru: A reaction takes place in a closed container. What does the balance show when it is over?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: While the container is closed, no atom escapes or is added. So mass is conserved.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Gas cannot escape from a closed container.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: No matter enters a closed container from outside.
cards.1.h: Why does mass change in an open container?
cards.1.p: When wood burns in the open, the ash left behind is lighter, because CO<sub>2</sub> and water vapor escape into the air. When magnesium burns, the product gets heavier, because oxygen from the air joins it. In both cases conservation still holds.
cards.1.key: If the balance changes with an open container, a gas has escaped or joined from the air.
cards.2.p: According to Proust, the mass ratio of the elements in a compound is fixed. In water, 1 g of hydrogen always combines with 8 g of oxygen. In Fe2O3, the mass ratio of Fe to O is 112:48, or 7:3.
cards.2.svg#13: The ratio is the same whatever the source or amount
cards.2.key: The Fe:O ratio comes from 2×56 : 3×16. Do not confuse the mass ratio with the ratio of atoms, like 2:1 in H₂O.
cards.3.h: Calculation: which substance is left over?
cards.3.p: Say 3 g of hydrogen reacts with 40 g of oxygen. The ratio is 1:8, so the hydrogen combines with only 24 g of oxygen. That leaves 16 g of oxygen, and 27 g of water forms.
cards.3.etk.soru: Hydrogen and oxygen combine in a 1 : 8 mass ratio. Change the masses: which one is left over, and how much water forms?
cards.3.key: Divide each mass by its ratio number. The substance that gives the smaller result is used up completely.
cards.4.h: A fixed ratio on a graph
cards.4.p: If you plot the oxygen used against the hydrogen, you get a straight line through the origin, and its slope is 8. For example, 2 g of hydrogen combines with 16 g of oxygen to form 18 g of water.
cards.4.svg#10: 2 g H + 16 g O = 18 g water
cards.4.key: Every point on the line gives the same compound. The slope is the ratio of the mass of oxygen to the mass of hydrogen.
cards.5.p: Two elements can form more than one compound. According to Dalton, when the mass of one element is held fixed, the masses of the other give a ratio of small whole numbers. For example, CO has 16 g of oxygen and CO2 has 32 g.
cards.5.key: For 12 g of carbon, the masses of oxygen are 16:32, or 1:2. First make the shared element equal, then compare the other element.
cards.6.p: It is the same for nitrogen oxides. 14 g of nitrogen combines with 16 g of oxygen in NO and with 32 g in NO<sub>2</sub>, a ratio of 1:2. If the number of atoms of the shared element is equal, you can read the ratio from the numbers of atoms.
cards.6.svg#17: = mass ratio of O for the same nitrogen
cards.6.key: In N₂O, NO and NO₂, the masses of oxygen for 28 g of nitrogen are in a 1:2:4 ratio.
cards.6.once.soru: Between N₂O and NO₂, what is the ratio of oxygen masses for equal nitrogen?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: If you equalize nitrogen, the compounds become N₂O and N₂O₄. The ratio of oxygen atoms is 1 : 4.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: You must first make the numbers of nitrogen atoms equal.
cards.7.h: When is there no multiple proportion?
cards.7.p: A multiple proportion is looked for only between different compounds of the same two elements. For compounds with the same empirical formula, such as N2O4 and NO2, the ratio comes out 1:1, and this does not count as a multiple proportion.
cards.7.key: The empirical formula is the simplest ratio of the atoms. C₂H₂ and C₆H₆ also share the same empirical formula (CH). There is no multiple proportion between different masses of the same compound.
cards.7.once.soru: Between which pair is there a multiple proportion?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: These are two separate compounds that the same two elements form in different ratios.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: They have the same empirical formula (NO₂), and the ratio comes out 1:1.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.yazi: 5 g of water and 50 g of water
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: These are the same compound, so there is no multiple proportion to look for.
cards.8.p: According to Gay-Lussac, at the same temperature and pressure gas volumes combine in small whole-number ratios. For example, 2 L of hydrogen combines with 1 L of oxygen to form 2 L of water vapor.
cards.8.svg#11: at the same T and P (above 100 °C at 1 atm)
cards.8.svg#12: 3 L gas → 2 L gas: volume is not conserved
cards.8.key: 3 L of gas went down to 2 L. Mass is always conserved, but the total volume of gas may not be.
cards.9.p: According to Avogadro, at the same temperature and pressure equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules. So the volume ratio equals the ratio of molecules. H2 and Cl2 are diatomic molecules.
cards.9.svg#6: At the same T and P, equal volume = equal particles
cards.9.key: Equal volume means equal numbers of particles. But this holds only at the same temperature and pressure.
cards.9.once.soru: At the same temperature and pressure, which has more molecules: 1 L of hydrogen or 1 L of oxygen?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: Under the same conditions, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: A heavier molecule does not change the number.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: A lighter molecule does not change the number.
cards.10.p: Dalton explained these laws with his atomic theory. In his view, elements are made of atoms, atoms combine in small whole-number ratios, and they are not destroyed in a reaction. The idea that atoms cannot be divided no longer holds today.
cards.10.svg#4: Atoms of an element are identical
cards.10.svg#7: Compound: combining in small whole-number ratios
cards.10.key: You saw in the topic on atomic models that atoms can be divided and that isotopes exist. But the idea that atoms are conserved in reactions still holds today.
cards.10.once.soru: Which part of Dalton's atomic theory no longer holds today?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: We know that atoms are made of protons, neutrons and electrons.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: This idea still holds today, and conservation of mass rests on it.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: This idea still holds today, and formulas rest on it.
cards.11.p:
• In a closed container the total mass is conserved.
• In a compound the mass ratio is fixed. In water H:O is 1:8.
• By the law of multiple proportions, when the shared element is held fixed, the masses of the other are in small whole-number ratios.
• At the same temperature and pressure, gas volumes combine in whole-number ratios.
• Atoms can be divided, and isotopes exist.
cards.11.svg#1: mass is conserved in a closed container
quiz.0.q: Nitrogen and oxygen form two different compounds. For 7 g of nitrogen, 4 g of oxygen bonds in the first compound and 16 g in the second. How many times the oxygen mass in the first is the oxygen mass in the second?
quiz.0.e: Nitrogen is fixed at 7 g in both compounds. The oxygen masses are 4 : 16, or 1 : 4. This is the law of multiple proportions, and the compounds are N₂O and NO₂.
quiz.1.q: Sort each pair by whether a multiple proportion can be looked for between them.
quiz.1.e: A multiple proportion is looked for between compounds of the same two elements with different empirical formulas. H<sub>2</sub>O and H<sub>2</sub>S do not share two elements, NO<sub>2</sub> and N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> have the same empirical formula, and 5 g and 50 g of water are the same compound.
quiz.2.q: In water, 1 g of hydrogen always combines with 8 g of oxygen. 12 g of hydrogen and 64 g of oxygen react to form water. When the reaction is complete, how many grams of water have formed?
quiz.2.e: 64 g of oxygen combines with 64 ÷ 8 = 8 g of hydrogen. 8 + 64 = 72 g of water forms, and 12 − 8 = 4 g of hydrogen is left over.
quiz.3.q: At the same temperature and pressure, 2 L of H₂ and 1 L of O₂ react completely to form water vapor. Which is true?
quiz.3.o.0: The total gas volume stays 3 L
quiz.3.e: The volumes are in a 2:1:2 ratio, and 3 L of gas turns into 2 L of water vapor. Volume is not conserved, but mass always is.
quiz.3.y.0: Gas volumes do not simply add up. By the ratio 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 3 L of gas turns into 2 L of vapor.
quiz.3.y.1: Volume can go down, but mass is conserved in every reaction. Atoms do not disappear.
quiz.3.y.2: Volumes follow the mole ratio. By the equation 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 2 L of H₂ forms 2 L of vapor.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Burn magnesium, make water and combine gas volumes.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Lavoisier showed that in reactions in a closed container the total mass does not change. But what if the container is open? You will burn a magnesium ribbon in an open dish on a balance.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: When the magnesium burns and turns into a white powder, what does the balance show?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: When wood burns the ash gets lighter, because CO₂ and water vapor escape into the air. With magnesium no gas escapes. Instead, a gas joins from the air.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Magnesium combines with oxygen from the air (2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO). 1.6 g of oxygen joins 2.4 g of magnesium, and the balance shows 4.0 g. Mass was conserved, because oxygen from the air came onto the balance.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: That would be true in a closed container. Here the container is open. Think about whether something from the air joins what is on the balance.
A:adimlar.1.metin: According to Proust, the mass ratio of elements in a compound is fixed. In water, the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen is 1 : 8. The container holds 40 g of oxygen. Add just enough hydrogen to turn all of it into water.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: 5 g of hydrogen combines with 40 g of oxygen, because 5 : 40 = 1 : 8. The water formed is 5 + 40 = 45 g. Add less hydrogen and oxygen is left over. Add more and hydrogen is left over.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Now the container holds 10 g of hydrogen and 40 g of oxygen. The ratio is 1 : 8, so one is used up completely and the other is left over.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: What is left over when the reaction is done?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: 40 / 8 = 5 g of hydrogen is enough to use up all the oxygen. No oxygen is left over.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: For nothing to be left over, the masses would have to be in a 1 : 8 ratio. Here the ratio is 10 : 40, or 1 : 4.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: 40 g of oxygen combines with only 5 g of hydrogen. 5 g of hydrogen is left over, and 45 g of water forms. Since 10 + 40 = 45 + 5, mass is still conserved.
A:adimlar.3.baslik: A fixed ratio on a graph
A:adimlar.3.metin: If you plot the oxygen used against the hydrogen, you get a straight line through the origin. Slide the point and find the one that gives 27 g of water.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: 3 g of hydrogen and 24 g of oxygen combine to form 27 g of water. The mass of water is 9 times the hydrogen, because 1 + 8 = 9. The amount changes, but the ratio does not.
A:adimlar.4.metin: Carbon and oxygen form two different compounds, CO and CO₂. Keep carbon fixed at 12 g in both and compare the masses of oxygen.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: For 12 g of carbon, what is the ratio of the oxygen masses in CO and CO₂?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The oxygen masses are not equal. Show CO₂ too and compare the two bars.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Check the order. CO (16 g) comes first, then CO₂ (32 g).
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: 16 : 32 = 1 : 2. When the shared element is held fixed, the masses of the other are in a small whole-number ratio. This is called Dalton's law of multiple proportions.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Gay-Lussac found that at the same temperature and pressure, gases combine in small whole-number ratios by volume. The container holds 1 L of oxygen. Add just enough hydrogen that no gas is left over, and play it.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: 2 L of hydrogen and 1 L of oxygen combined to form 2 L of water vapor. The total volume went down from 3 L to 2 L. Mass is always conserved, but gas volume may not be. According to Avogadro, equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules, so the volume ratio is the ratio of molecules.
A:kapanis.0: In a closed container the total mass is conserved (Lavoisier). If the balance changes with an open container, a gas has escaped or joined from the air.
A:kapanis.1: According to Proust, the mass ratio in a compound is fixed. In water H : O is 1 : 8. The substance present beyond the ratio is left over.
A:kapanis.2: By Dalton's law of multiple proportions, when the shared element is held fixed, the masses of the other are in a small whole-number ratio. In CO and CO₂ this ratio is 1 : 2.
A:kapanis.3: By Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes, at the same temperature and pressure gases combine in whole-number ratios by volume. The total volume may not be conserved.
A:kapanis.4: According to Avogadro, at the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases hold equal numbers of particles.
